title: bat line buffers input while cat does not, and tail -f recipe doesn't mention the issue
body:
**What steps will reproduce the bug?**

I use log files in append mode with line buffering disabled in the program under test during development.
With cat this command immediately outputs partial lines:

```
'tail' -f /tmp/myLog | 'cat'  --number
```

But this corresponding bat command doesn't:

```
'tail' -f /tmp/myLog | '/home/<user>/.cargo/bin/bat'  --paging=never
```

To reproduce this the program under test can be simulated using e.g. `echo -n partialLine`.

Appending a newline to /tmp/myLog (e.g. with `echo '' >>/tmp/myLog`) causes the buffered stuff to finally get displayed by bat.  So it looks like bat line buffers its input, while cat doesn't.  Is there a way to make bat show stuff immediately like cat?

The `tail -f` recipe on the main doc page should be changed to indicate how if it's possible, or mention the problem if its not possible.

**How did you install `bat`?**

`cargo install --locked bat`

**bat version and environment**

$ /home/<user>/.cargo/bin/bat --pager=never --diagnostic

comments.body: Adding `-l log` to the bat command as advised in the recipe doesn't fix the problem.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> Adding `-l log` to the bat command as advised in the recipe doesn't fix the problem.

Definitely syntax highlighting is incompatible with no line buffering, because there is no way to tell whether something should be highlighted a certain way until you know what comes after it - i.e. what looks like a keyword may just be the incomplete start of a longer word which could just be a variable or function call etc.

We have [this in the manpage](https://github.com/sharkdp/bat/blob/master/assets/manual/bat.1.in#L264-L267), but I suspect it's not quite true - `bat` currently always buffers at line level. Initially so it can guess the syntax and encoding, detect if it is binary or text etc.
So it may be that we would need a special flag to skip all that and just stream the input...

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Could you get (most of) the best of both worlds by waiting a bit for a full line (and doing all the lovely fancy bat stuff if you get it) then giving up and sending the input along without it?  Or an option to do that?  If an option then it would be opt-in and so wouldn't even seem like sometimes surprising appearance of highlight fail.

This would allow fearless use of bat in shell functions/aliases/abbreviations etc.

I notice this is how tail -f works anyway.  From tail man page:

```
-s, --sleep-interval=N
              with  -f,  sleep  for approximately N seconds (default 1.0)
              between iterations; with inotify and --pid=P, check process
              P at least once every N seconds
```

I'd probably try a much shorter time, since two seconds delay might end up being noticeable and distracting in some situations (I've never noticed the up to 1 second tail -f apparently adds).

I was quite interested in this topic and had a look. 

I found that in input.rs the function read_line() has a read_until() call on the dyn BufRead object (lines 260-320) . This is the reason why it blocks and would not output partial lines.

I experimented around a littlebit and was able to get it working with using the fill_buf() and consume() functionality of the BufRead.

My problem is that the calling function in controller.rs (line 277) handles buffering of read lines and then forwards them to a printer object.

My hope that if the printer receives a line with the same line number as before it would overwrite that line. Unfortunately that does not happen.

Does someone with more knowledge in this project know how i could print lines overwriting the previously printed partial lines?

I will continue trying to find a way but i was wondering if someone with more previous experience in this project might already know a way to do this.

(i am implementing this on my fork on the 'bat_partial_line_buffering' branch if anyone is interested in helping me)

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Hi i looked a littlebit into it today to and came to the conclusion that its borderline impossible (at least for me). 

In src/printer.rs line ~600 print_line() is getting called. I was looking into manipulating the chars and counting how many have been written to the current partial line, and storing it somewhere as a state for the next call to complete the lines and wrap correctly. 

While doing this i encountered a problem where stdout just stopped getting flushed until the piped input included a '\n' or i had called a println!() for debugging purposes.

Finding the source of this led me to believe this whole feature request to be borderline impossible. One of the Paramter for the print_line() function is a 'OutputHandle' (coding/bat/src/output.rs l. 222) which is an enum over 2 Varians, references to either '&'a mut dyn io::Write' or '&'a mut dyn fmt::Write'.

The first sentence of the documentation for fmt::Write is 'This trait only accepts UTF-8–encoded data and is not [flushable]'.

Therefore we cannot write unfinished lines to the printer as they couldnt be flushed.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Well thanks for looking at it.  It sounds like adding a mention of the issue to the recipe on the main page might be the thing to do.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
👋 This issue was identified by [Token Steward](https://github.com/participant3/Token-Steward) as high-impact. I'd like to contribute a fix — here's the proposed approach before writing any code.

## Proposed approach

**Problem:** `bat` line-buffers input via `read_until(b'\n')`, blocking until a newline arrives. This prevents streaming use cases like `tail -f | bat` from showing partial lines.

**Solution:** Repurpose the existing `--unbuffered`/`-u` flag (currently ignored) to use `fill_buf()`/`consume()` instead of `read_until`. This returns whatever data the OS has available, even without a trailing newline. Complete lines get full bat treatment; partial lines are printed and flushed immediately.

**Trade-offs:**
- Partial lines get their own line number/decorations
- Syntax highlighting may be imperfect on partial lines
- First line still blocks (content detection needs it)

**Files touched:** `config.rs`, `input.rs`, `output.rs`, `controller.rs`, `clap_app.rs`, `app.rs`, man page, shell completions, tests

Would you welcome this contribution? Any feedback on the approach before I proceed?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Sounds interesting, I believe we would welcome such an approach, especially if the changes have no effect when the unbuffered command line switch is unused. I wonder if it would make sense to automatically disable line numbering in unbuffered mode, to prevent confusion. Also, I wonder how the output would look in practice - would there be many 1 character partial lines etc which would essentially be unreadable?
I also wonder how to write good integration tests for it, it sounds like the output would be deterministic...

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Thanks for the feedback @participant1!

**Line numbering:** Great suggestion. I'll auto-disable line numbers in unbuffered mode to avoid confusion. Users could still force them with `--style=numbers` if needed.

**Output readability:** `fill_buf()` returns whatever chunk the OS has buffered from the pipe writer, so the granularity matches what the upstream process flushes. `echo -n "partial line" >> /tmp/log` would arrive as one `"partial line"` chunk, not character-by-character.

**Integration tests:** We can get deterministic output by controlling the input. For unit tests, a custom `BufRead` implementation that returns specific chunks from `fill_buf()` works well. For integration tests, a pipe with controlled writes from a child process. I'll include both in the PR.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Sorry for the late response to this.

From the description it sounds like there's still probably an issue with respect to my use case that caused this report (instrumentation debugging).  Unfortunately buffering the first line still has the potential to result in a lot of confusion, since there often isn't much output in instrumentation debugging.  If I understand the proposed fix correctly it could result in a situation where the creation of a new log or path or instrumentation change in the program under test would cause buffering in bat as before.  To completely fix the problem the first line would need to be passed through as well, or a warning of some sort produced.

I previously created a small shim to go in pipelines and eliminate any possible confusion:

https://codeberg.org/reporter/unterminated_line_catcher

It looks like this shim is simple enough that e.g. Gemeni-3 gets it entirely right (there's an AI version in the repo) but I didn't inspect or test that version carefully.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: The problem isn't at all to get the lines, the problem is that the functions that is responsible for correctly printing the input in a formatted way and syntax highlighted way expects a full line and the printer used in bat as a general only flushes when a new line is encountered and doesn't have a manual flush method, so it's not possible to force the printer to flush before reading a full line.
